events.content: STRATEGY: ASSERT. The room has just opened. I'll start by sharing the current situation here in Singapore. The PSI is in the unhealthy range again, which is my main worry right now because of my mother's asthma and the kids. It's a factual way to begin.
Morning everyone. The air here is not good again. The app already shows unhealthy.
Waiting for others to join the conversation.
STRATEGY: ASSERT. Kelvin is right, the air is bad. It's the same here in Johor. I'm really worried about my son's school. If they close it again, what am I going to do? I have to work.
Morning. It's the same here. I'm just hoping my son's school doesn't close.
I've shared my immediate concern.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Kelvin and Farhana are talking about unhealthy air and schools maybe closing. My sister's family in Kalimantan is living in a much worse situation right now. Her kids are sick. I should share this to show how bad it is at the source.
It's worse where my sister is, in Kalimantan. The sky is yellow and her children are coughing all the time.
I've shared my family's situation.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Budi's story about his sister's children coughing is concerning. Farhana was also worried about her son's school closing. My daughter's kindergarten was actually closed because of the haze. I can share this to show that her worries are justified and it's happening here too.
My daughter's school was closed for two days this week. We had to do home-based learning.
I've shared my experience.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Nur Aqilah's daughter's school already closed. That's exactly what I'm afraid is going to happen here. If my kids' school closes, it's going to be a real problem for my wife and me to arrange work. It makes the whole situation feel much closer to home.
That's what I'm worried about. Home-based learning is not easy to manage when you're also trying to work.
Shared my concern about school closures.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Kelvin is echoing the exact problem I faced this week. It's not just a worry for him, it was my reality. I should agree with him and confirm how difficult it actually is to manage work and home-based learning.
Tell me about it. It was really hard to get any work done.
I've responded to Kelvin, agreeing with his point.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Nur Aqilah and Kelvin are talking about exactly what I'm worried about. If my son's school closes, it's a huge problem for my job. I can't work from home. I should explain my situation.
That's it. I have to take leave if the school is closed. I can't work from home from the factory.
I have explained my specific difficulty.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Farhana is talking about losing income if she has to take leave. It's the same for me. I'm a motorbike driver. If I don't work, I don't get paid. I should share this. It shows how this haze problem isn't just about health, it's about our daily survival.
Same for me. If I don't ride, my family doesn't eat. I'm out on the road all day in this.
I've shared how the haze affects my work.

It is now Friday 18 September 2026. Air quality is unhealthy at half of Malaysia's 68 monitoring stations, and the haze reached southern Vietnam on 14 September. Malaysia has offered Indonesia one firefighting plane, three helicopters and 52 personnel. Japan has sent military helicopters to help Indonesia fight the fires. Indonesian police say 95 companies are being investigated over the fires, along with many individuals. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. It's been two weeks and the news says the haze is still bad, even spreading. My main concern is still my daughter. The situation hasn't really improved for us either. I should share what our daily life is like now, this constant worry.
It feels like it's not getting any better. We're still checking the air quality every day before letting my daughter play outside.
Shared my update on the situation.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Nur Aqilah is describing exactly what I'm doing. It's this constant checking, the daily worry. It shows we're all in the same situation. I'll confirm that I'm doing the same, and mention my mother again since that's my main concern.
Same here. I'm checking the app all the time. My mother's asthma is not good in this weather.
Shared my agreement and primary concern.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Kelvin's worry about his mother's asthma makes me think about my own son. Children are vulnerable too. This air is terrible for his little lungs. I am constantly worried he'll get sick from it.
Yes, I worry about that too. The children and the old people. It's scary to think of my son breathing this every day.
I've shared my concern about my son's health, relating it to Kelvin's point.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Farhana is worried about her son breathing this. For my sister's kids in Kalimantan, it's not a worry, it's already happened. They are sick because of the smoke. I need to make the others understand how bad it is at the source.
They are sick. My sister took them to the doctor. It's the smoke. She wants to leave but they can't just go.
I have explained the direct health consequences for my family.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's news about his sister's children being sick from the smoke is terrible. It makes my own worries about my daughter feel much more real. All our concerns about health aren't just hypotheticals anymore.
That's terrible. I'm so sorry to hear that. I hope they feel better soon.
Expressed sympathy for Budi's family.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Nur Aqilah is being nice, but her sympathy doesn't change the situation. I appreciate her saying that, but the problem isn't going away. I want to express that the cycle of sickness is frustrating and seems endless because the cause is still there.
Thanks. The doctor gives medicine, but they just breathe the same air again. It doesn't stop.
I've responded to Nur Aqilah's sympathy by highlighting the ongoing problem.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Budi's point about the medicine is exactly my fear. It highlights the futility of it all. My mother has her inhalers, but what good are they if the air itself is the problem? The real need is for clean air, not just medicine to treat the symptoms. It's a cycle that won't stop unless the source of the haze is dealt with.
That's exactly it. The doctors can give medicine, but it's no use if they just go out and breathe the same air again.
Expressed my agreement and frustration about the situation's hopelessness.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Kelvin is right, the problem isn't something a doctor's visit can fix. We're all just breathing this in constantly. It makes me feel so helpless about my son. We make him wear a mask, but how much can a little mask do when the whole sky is grey? It feels like we're fighting a losing battle.
You're right. We have the masks and all, but it feels like it's not enough. How can it be enough, against all this smoke?
I've shared my feeling of helplessness.

It is now Friday 9 October 2026. On 7 October Greenpeace Malaysia published a list of the 20 entities most linked to this year's fires in Indonesia; it includes Malaysian and Singaporean companies. All schools in Johor have been closed since 7 October, and today schools were also ordered closed in Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya. In Singapore the 24-hour PSI reached 192 this evening, the highest this year, on the weekend of the Formula One Grand Prix, which is going ahead. Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said he had called Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto, who agreed to take the necessary steps. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. The new report says Malaysian and Singaporean companies are also responsible for the fires. This is important. It's not just Indonesia's fault. Everyone always blames us, but now there's proof that companies from their own countries are part of the problem. I need to bring this up.
So it's not just our companies. I see Malaysian and Singaporean companies are also on that list from Greenpeace.
I have pointed out the shared responsibility for the fires based on the new information.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Budi's point about the Greenpeace list is valid, but it just highlights how complex and frustrating this is. It feels like everyone is pointing fingers, but for my family, the problem is the same no matter who is to blame. The smoke is still here. I want to express that helplessness and bring the focus back to the impact on us.
It doesn't matter whose companies they are. We're all still breathing the same bad air.
Expressed my frustration about the situation.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Nur Aqilah is right, it doesn't matter who is to blame when we are all suffering. The air quality here is terrible, the worst it's been this year. It feels absurd that a huge event like the F1 is going ahead while we're all being told to stay indoors. I'll point out this contradiction.
She's right. The air here is terrible tonight, worst it's been all year. And they're still having the F1.
Shared my frustration about the current air quality and the F1 race.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Kelvin is talking about the F1 race. That seems so unimportant compared to what's happening here. All the schools in Johor are closed. My son is at home, and I've had to take time off work. This is a real crisis for my family, not just bad air for a sports event. I need to explain how serious this is for me.
They're still having a race? Here, all the schools are closed. Since Wednesday. I had to take leave from the factory. I don't know what we will do if this goes on.
I've shared the direct impact of the haze on my life and work.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Farhana is worried about losing income because she has to take leave. I completely understand that. I'm a driver, I work outside all day. The haze directly impacts my ability to earn money for my family. It's the same problem she's facing. I should share my situation to show that we're in the same boat.
Same here. I'm a driver. If I don't work, we don't eat. I have to be out in this all day.
I've shared how the haze affects my own livelihood, connecting with Farhana's concern.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's situation is just as difficult as mine, maybe even harder. He has to work outside in this, while I'm worried about not being able to work at all because the schools are closed. We're both stuck between our health and our jobs. 'If I don't work, we don't eat.' I feel that. It's the same for me.
Yes, it's the same for us. If I can't go to the factory, there's no money. At least I'm inside, though. It must be so hard for you, having to be out driving in the smoke all day.
I've responded to Budi and shared my perspective.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Farhana and Budi are talking about how they have to risk their health to earn money. It's a much harder situation than mine. While I found it difficult to work with my daughter at home, I didn't have to worry about losing my pay. Their situation is really tough. I want to show that I understand and sympathise with the impossible choices they're facing.
It's so difficult for everyone. We all have to make these impossible choices.
Shared my empathy for the difficult situations everyone is in.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Nur Aqilah summed it up perfectly. We're all having to choose between our health and our jobs. I'm in the same boat. Part of my work is outdoors, so I'm exposed. It's a constant worry.
Exactly. My job is partly outdoors at the warehouse. I can't just not go to work.
Shared my own work difficulty.

It is now Tuesday 13 October 2026. On 10 October the head of Indonesia's Government Communications Agency, Syahganda Nainggolan, said the fires were "beyond human error; this is truly nature" and added: "We're not just sending over the haze. When there's no haze, we send oxygen. The oxygen from Singapore and Malaysia is from our forests, right?" A video of the remark is being widely shared. Indonesia's disaster agency said ground personnel are preferred to aircraft from neighbours. On 11 October Malaysia said it had still had no reply to its offer of help. On 12 October President Prabowo ordered maximum efforts against the fires. Today a Malaysian MP told Parliament that Malaysians should boycott companies linked to the burning ("We need to hit them where they hurt the most") and that banks should stop financing them. Malaysia's Firefly airline has cancelled flights to Singapore because of the haze. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. That comment from the Indonesian official about sending oxygen... that's just insulting. Is he joking? While my son can't go to school and I'm worried about my job? It makes me so angry. The idea about boycotting the companies, though, that sounds like a good idea. It feels like finally something we can do.
Sending oxygen? Is he joking? Our schools are still closed. I think that MP is right, we should boycott all these companies.
I've reacted to the latest news with anger and support for the boycott idea.

STRATEGY: CHALLENGE. Farhana is angry and supporting a boycott. I understand the anger, especially after that stupid 'sending oxygen' comment from our government official, which is just embarrassing. But a boycott... that's a big step. It's easy for a politician in Malaysia to say that, but these companies employ a lot of people here in Indonesia. If they get boycotted and lose money, or shut down, it's the ordinary workers who will suffer. People will lose their jobs. That's a real problem that affects families like mine. I need to point out this practical difficulty.
A boycott is easy for them to say. But those companies have so many workers here. What happens to all the people who will lose their jobs?
I have expressed my practical concerns about the proposed boycott.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi is right. Farhana is angry and wants to do something, but a boycott isn't simple. It would just create more problems for ordinary people who need those jobs. It feels like there are no good solutions, just one bad choice after another.
That's true. It's always the ordinary people who get caught in the middle.
I've agreed with Budi's point about the complexity of a boycott.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Nur Aqilah is right. We're the ones paying the price for all this. Budi has a point about the boycott hurting workers, and she's right that it's always the ordinary people who get caught. We're stuck choosing between our health and our jobs. It's a no-win situation.
That's right. We have to work, but we also have to breathe. It feels like we have no good choices.
Agreed with Nur Aqilah's sentiment.

STRATEGY: CONCEDE. Budi has a good point about the boycott. I was just so angry at that official's comment, but Budi is right. If companies are boycotted, it's the workers, people like us, who will suffer. Kelvin's right, there are no good choices here for any of us.
You're right, Budi. I was just angry. A boycott would just hurt more ordinary people.
I've reconsidered my position on the boycott after hearing Budi's point.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Farhana agrees with me now, which is good. She sees that a boycott would hurt people like us. Her anger is understandable, especially after that stupid 'sending oxygen' comment from our government official. It's embarrassing and makes it harder to talk about the real problems. I should show I understand why she was angry.
Yes. And that 'sending oxygen' comment doesn't help. It makes all of us look bad.
I have acknowledged Farhana's point and shared frustration.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi is right to be frustrated with that official's comment. It's not helpful at all and just creates more bad feelings between countries when we're all suffering from the same problem. It shows how out of touch some leaders are. The problem isn't the people, it's the lack of proper action from the top.
That kind of talk doesn't help anyone. We're all just trying to get through this.
I've responded to Budi's comment.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Nur Aqilah is right, the political talk is useless. That 'sending oxygen' comment from the Indonesian official was particularly galling. It's like they're not taking our suffering seriously at all. It's not a game; my mother has asthma and this is a real health crisis for my family.
Yeah, that 'sending oxygen' comment. Makes you wonder if they think this is a game. My mother has asthma. It's not a game for her.
Expressed my frustration about the official's comment.

It is now Friday 16 October 2026. On 14 October fine-particle pollution in western Singapore reached its highest level since 2015; Singapore has opened haze shelters, is giving out N95 masks and some schools have stopped outdoor activities. Timor-Leste closed its schools. Indonesian police named 223 people and nine companies as suspects. On 15 October Indonesia's Foreign Minister said Indonesia would now accept foreign firefighting help, and Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore was checking which companies were responsible and that legal action could follow. Today Singapore's Minister Grace Fu announced that notices had been sent to seven Indonesian companies under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act; some lawyers said this could have diplomatic consequences. Singapore's 24-hour PSI reached 229 today, the very unhealthy range, the 12th day in a row of unhealthy air. The haze has reached Jakarta. Malaysia's government said no Malaysian plantation companies were involved in the fires. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. The news is a lot to take in. Singapore is finally taking legal action, which feels like something concrete might happen. That's a bit of hope. But our own government just says 'it's not us'. The smoke is still here, so that doesn't help me much. It's good Indonesia is accepting help now, but it feels so late.

At least Singapore is trying to do something now, sending notices to those companies. Maybe that will finally make a difference. It's good that Indonesia is accepting help, but they should have done that weeks ago.
I've shared my reaction to the latest news.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Farhana is right. The government should have accepted help a long time ago. It's frustrating to see them moving so slowly while people are getting sick. My sister's family is still suffering, and now the haze has reached Jakarta, so it's affecting my health and my work too. I agree with her frustration.
You're right. It's been weeks. My sister's children are still sick. Now the smoke is here too.
I've agreed with Farhana and shared how the delay is affecting my family and me personally.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's comment about his sister's sick children is heartbreaking. As a mother, I can feel his anxiety. It's the children who are suffering the most, and it's been going on for so long. It makes my own worries about my daughter feel so much more real.
I'm so sorry to hear they're still sick. It's the children I worry about most too.
Expressed my sympathy for Budi's family.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. Nur Aqilah's right, the children are a big part of this. My own kids are being affected directly. Their school has stopped outdoor activities. This is a concrete example of how bad it is here now, and it adds to my worry. I'll share this to show it's not just an abstract problem for us.
Yes, it's the same for me. My kids' school has stopped all their outdoor activities. They're just stuck inside.
Shared how the haze is affecting my own children.
STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Kelvin's describing exactly what's happening with my son too. It's frustrating for the kids to be cooped up inside. And for us parents, it's a constant worry.
Same here. I'm just glad my son's school hasn't closed again, but he can't go outside to play. It's really hard on them.
I've agreed with Kelvin and shared my similar situation.
STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Farhana's saying exactly what I'm feeling. It's the same here. The kids are getting restless being cooped up all day. It's not healthy for them in another way.
Yeah, exactly. Mine are climbing the walls at home. It's tough.
Shared my agreement with Farhana.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Everyone is talking about being stuck inside. For me, it's the opposite. My work is outside. I don't have the choice to stay home. I have to go out in this smoke to earn money for my family. This is a different kind of problem.
It's hard when you have to be outside. My job is on the road all day, in the smoke.
I've explained my personal difficulty.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi has to work outside in the smoke all day. That must be very unhealthy and worrying for him and his family. I'm lucky that I work in an office, so I'm protected from the worst of it during the day. His situation highlights how dangerous this is for people who don't have that choice.
That must be awful. I can't imagine having to be out in it all day. Please take care.
I've expressed my concern for Budi.

It is now Wednesday 21 October 2026. On 19 October Singapore's Minister K. Shanmugam said the Singapore Exchange was questioning seven Singapore-listed agriculture companies about links to the fires (Golden Agri-Resources, Bumitama Agri, First Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri Resources and TSH Resources), that the government was also looking at Asia Pulp and Paper, and that notices had gone to three more Indonesian companies, ten in all. He said: "We will pursue this matter for as long as it takes" and "The Indonesian public is suffering as well." The same day a former Indonesian trade minister, Muhammad Lutfi, said four of the seven Indonesian companies had Singapore ties and challenged Singapore to raid their offices. Today President Prabowo said there were indications that foreign companies were involved in the fires, and Malaysia's deputy environment minister said Malaysia was open to a haze law like Singapore's. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. All this news is about governments and companies pointing fingers at each other. Singapore says this, Indonesia says that. It doesn't help me. I still have to breathe this air to make a living. My family is still sick. It's just big talk that doesn't change the reality for people like us.
So now it's a fight between the governments. It's all just talk. For us here, nothing changes. The smoke is still here.
I've expressed my frustration with the political back-and-forth.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's frustration is understandable. It does feel like the governments are just arguing with each other while we are the ones who are still breathing in this smoke. It doesn't seem to be getting any better for us.
He's right. All this talk doesn't make the air any cleaner for us.
I've agreed with Budi's point.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. I agree with Budi and Nur Aqilah. This back and forth between the governments is just talk. Naming companies is one thing, but it doesn't change the fact that the air is still unhealthy for my family right now. The problem is here and now, not in some future legal battle.
Right. They can point fingers and name all the companies they want. But we're the ones breathing this air today. It doesn't make a difference to us on the ground.
Expressed my frustration with the lack of immediate action.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Kelvin is right. It's all just talk between governments. For me, it's the same worry every day. Will the school be open? Will I have to take leave from my job? This political drama doesn't change that.
Exactly. It doesn't help me figure out if I can send my son to school tomorrow, or if I have to try and take another day off work.
I've shared how the political talk doesn't solve my immediate, practical problems.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Farhana's point about work and school is exactly my situation. It's a daily stress. For me, it's not just the kids, but also my mother who has asthma. The unhealthy air is a direct threat to her health, which makes everything more stressful. I'll share that. It shows how personal and serious this is for my family.
Tell me about it. My mother has asthma. Every morning I'm checking the PSI, wondering if it's safe for her, if the kids' school will close. It's a constant worry.
Shared my personal worries about my mother's health and the daily uncertainty.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Kelvin brings up the health issue, his mother's asthma. That's a serious worry on top of everything else. It's not just the logistics of school closing, it's what this smoke is doing to our families' health. I feel the same way about my son.
Yes, it's the health part that's so worrying. My son doesn't have asthma, but I'm still scared about him breathing this air every single day.
I've shared my agreement and my own health concerns for my son.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. Farhana is worried about her son's health. Kelvin is worried about his mother's asthma and his kids. My sister's children are sick. This is the real problem for all of us. I have a baby daughter myself, so I share their fear completely. It's a constant worry.
Yes, I know what you mean. I have a baby daughter. I'm always worried about her.
Shared my personal worry about my daughter.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi is worried about his baby daughter. That's exactly how I feel about my five-year-old. It's this constant anxiety about what the smoke is doing to them. It's a shared fear among all of us who are parents.
Yes, exactly. I have a five-year-old. Every day I worry what this is doing to her.
Shared my own worries as a parent.

It is now Monday 26 October 2026. On 22 October Indonesia's energy minister, Bahlil Lahadalia, said Indonesia would reconsider energy exports to countries that do not respect it. On 24 October Indonesia cut its pipeline gas to Singapore by about 8 per cent of those exports, less than 2 per cent of Singapore's gas use, citing domestic needs. On 25 October Prime Minister Wong said Singapore expects all parties to honour their commitments. Today Bahlil said: "Do not lecture us, especially the energy ministry, on the importance of honoring contracts." Singapore's air has been back in the moderate range since 22 October, after 18 days of unhealthy air, and the first rains have fallen on Sumatra and Kalimantan. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. The news mentions more fighting between the governments, this time about gas. That doesn't help me. But it also says it has started to rain in Kalimantan. That's the first real good news. Rain can put out the fires and clear the air. This is what matters for my sister's family, and for us in Jakarta. This is the only part of the update that actually means anything for normal people.
Good. It's started raining. That's the real news. I hope it's enough.
I've shared my reaction, focusing on the positive news about the rain.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's right, the rain is the best news we've had. It's a huge relief to hear that. I've been so worried about my daughter, and this feels like a light at the end of the tunnel.
Yes, that's such a relief to hear. Let's hope it's enough to clear the air for good.
Expressed my relief about the rain.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. The rain is good news and the air is finally better here. It's a relief. But I've been through this before. A few days of rain doesn't mean the problem is over. I'm not getting my hopes up too high just yet. The air is 'moderate', not 'good'. I'll feel better when it's been clear for a while.
It's a relief for sure. Air is moderate here, not 'good' yet, but better. I'll feel better when it stays this way for more than a few days.
Shared my cautious optimism.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Kelvin is right. The rain is a relief, but it's not a solution yet. It's the same here, the air is probably a bit better but I won't feel secure until it's been clear for a good while. The worry about my son's school and my job isn't gone just because of one or two better days.
It's the same here. A relief, but I'm holding my breath to see if it lasts. It's hard to relax until you know the schools will stay open for good.
I've shared my cautious optimism and related it to my specific worries.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Farhana's point about not being able to relax is exactly right. It's the uncertainty. For me, it's not just about the schools, but also whether it's safe for my mother to even go to the market. This constant 'will it or won't it' is the most stressful part.
Exactly. You can't really make any plans. Every day you're wondering if it's safe for the old folks to go out, or if you'll get a message from the school again.
Agreed with Farhana's sentiment.
STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Kelvin has perfectly described the daily anxiety. That 'message from the school' is exactly what I dread. It throws my whole workday into chaos.
Yes, exactly. That one message from the school changes your whole plan for the day.
I've agreed with Kelvin's point and shared how it specifically affects me.

STRATEGY: EXPLAIN_NEED. They are talking about how one message from the school can change everything. For me, it's not about a message. It's about whether the air is safe enough for me to go out and work on my motorbike. The rain is a relief, but the worry about earning a living and about my family in Kalimantan doesn't just disappear overnight.
Yes, I understand. For me, it's checking the air quality every morning. Can I work today? Can I make enough money? The worry is still there.
I've shared how the haze personally affects my work and daily life.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's right. It's the daily uncertainty that's so stressful. You wake up and don't know if your day is going to be normal or completely disrupted. For him it's work and money, for me it was my daughter's school. It's the same feeling.
Yes, that's it. Every morning you just hope things can be normal.
I've shared my agreement with Budi's sentiment.

It is now Monday 16 November 2026. On 27 October Singapore's Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesia's Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir in Jakarta; they agreed to set up a joint task force to trace the money and corporate links of companies behind the fires, and direct ministerial hotlines. Arrmanatha said: "Smoke can cross borders, so can money." Rain put out most of the fires in late October, and Singapore ended its haze measures on 7 November. Singapore plans to push for an ASEAN coordinating centre on haze when it chairs ASEAN in 2027. Yesterday, at the ASEAN Summit in Manila, President Prabowo said: "I would like to apologise to my neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore. It is not our fault, but once again we apologise. But we have done our best." He said 17 company concessions had been revoked, 104 companies were under police investigation, 71,000 firefighters had been deployed and 16 people had died fighting the fires. The room has opened again.

STRATEGY: ASSERT. The news says the fires are out and our President has apologised. That's good. But the most important part for me is that 16 firefighters died. These people died trying to fix the problem. This is a real sacrifice. It's not just politics or talk. I want to point this out. It shows that Indonesians are suffering and fighting this too.
Thank God the fires are out. My sister says the air is clear now in Kalimantan. But to hear that 16 people died fighting them... That's the real cost.
I have shared my reaction to the latest news, focusing on the human cost.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Budi's news is terrible. 16 people died. It's easy to just be relieved the smoke is gone, but he's right to remind us of the real human cost. It puts all our own problems with the haze, like my daughter's school closing, into perspective. It's truly a tragedy.
That's awful. Yes, that's a terrible price to pay.
Acknowledged the tragic news.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. Sixteen people died fighting the fires. That's a terrible, sobering piece of news. While we were all worrying about our own families and daily lives, these people were on the front lines and lost everything. It really puts our own troubles into perspective. This is the real tragedy of the whole thing.
It's awful. You're right, that is the real cost. We worry about our families, but these people lost their lives.
Acknowledged the human cost of the fires.

STRATEGY: ACKNOWLEDGE. That is awful news. Hearing that people died fighting the fires is just terrible. It makes all my worries about my job and my son's school, as stressful as they were, feel so much smaller now. I should agree with them.

round_records.public_observation: It is now Friday 18 September 2026. Air quality is unhealthy at half of Malaysia's 68 monitoring stations, and the haze reached southern Vietnam on 14 September. Malaysia has offered Indonesia one firefighting plane, three helicopters and 52 personnel. Japan has sent military helicopters to help Indonesia fight the fires. Indonesian police say 95 companies are being investigated over the fires, along with many individuals. The room has opened again.

It is now Friday 9 October 2026. On 7 October Greenpeace Malaysia published a list of the 20 entities most linked to this year's fires in Indonesia; it includes Malaysian and Singaporean companies. All schools in Johor have been closed since 7 October, and today schools were also ordered closed in Melaka, Negeri Sembilan, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya. In Singapore the 24-hour PSI reached 192 this evening, the highest this year, on the weekend of the Formula One Grand Prix, which is going ahead. Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said he had called Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto, who agreed to take the necessary steps. The room has opened again.

It is now Tuesday 13 October 2026. On 10 October the head of Indonesia's Government Communications Agency, Syahganda Nainggolan, said the fires were "beyond human error; this is truly nature" and added: "We're not just sending over the haze. When there's no haze, we send oxygen. The oxygen from Singapore and Malaysia is from our forests, right?" A video of the remark is being widely shared. Indonesia's disaster agency said ground personnel are preferred to aircraft from neighbours. On 11 October Malaysia said it had still had no reply to its offer of help. On 12 October President Prabowo ordered maximum efforts against the fires. Today a Malaysian MP told Parliament that Malaysians should boycott companies linked to the burning ("We need to hit them where they hurt the most") and that banks should stop financing them. Malaysia's Firefly airline has cancelled flights to Singapore because of the haze. The room has opened again.

It is now Friday 16 October 2026. On 14 October fine-particle pollution in western Singapore reached its highest level since 2015; Singapore has opened haze shelters, is giving out N95 masks and some schools have stopped outdoor activities. Timor-Leste closed its schools. Indonesian police named 223 people and nine companies as suspects. On 15 October Indonesia's Foreign Minister said Indonesia would now accept foreign firefighting help, and Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore was checking which companies were responsible and that legal action could follow. Today Singapore's Minister Grace Fu announced that notices had been sent to seven Indonesian companies under Singapore's Transboundary Haze Pollution Act; some lawyers said this could have diplomatic consequences. Singapore's 24-hour PSI reached 229 today, the very unhealthy range, the 12th day in a row of unhealthy air. The haze has reached Jakarta. Malaysia's government said no Malaysian plantation companies were involved in the fires. The room has opened again.

It is now Wednesday 21 October 2026. On 19 October Singapore's Minister K. Shanmugam said the Singapore Exchange was questioning seven Singapore-listed agriculture companies about links to the fires (Golden Agri-Resources, Bumitama Agri, First Resources, Wilmar International, Kencana Agri, Indofood Agri Resources and TSH Resources), that the government was also looking at Asia Pulp and Paper, and that notices had gone to three more Indonesian companies, ten in all. He said: "We will pursue this matter for as long as it takes" and "The Indonesian public is suffering as well." The same day a former Indonesian trade minister, Muhammad Lutfi, said four of the seven Indonesian companies had Singapore ties and challenged Singapore to raid their offices. Today President Prabowo said there were indications that foreign companies were involved in the fires, and Malaysia's deputy environment minister said Malaysia was open to a haze law like Singapore's. The room has opened again.

It is now Monday 26 October 2026. On 22 October Indonesia's energy minister, Bahlil Lahadalia, said Indonesia would reconsider energy exports to countries that do not respect it. On 24 October Indonesia cut its pipeline gas to Singapore by about 8 per cent of those exports, less than 2 per cent of Singapore's gas use, citing domestic needs. On 25 October Prime Minister Wong said Singapore expects all parties to honour their commitments. Today Bahlil said: "Do not lecture us, especially the energy ministry, on the importance of honoring contracts." Singapore's air has been back in the moderate range since 22 October, after 18 days of unhealthy air, and the first rains have fallen on Sumatra and Kalimantan. The room has opened again.

It is now Monday 16 November 2026. On 27 October Singapore's Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan met Indonesia's Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir in Jakarta; they agreed to set up a joint task force to trace the money and corporate links of companies behind the fires, and direct ministerial hotlines. Arrmanatha said: "Smoke can cross borders, so can money." Rain put out most of the fires in late October, and Singapore ended its haze measures on 7 November. Singapore plans to push for an ASEAN coordinating centre on haze when it chairs ASEAN in 2027. Yesterday, at the ASEAN Summit in Manila, President Prabowo said: "I would like to apologise to my neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore. It is not our fault, but once again we apologise. But we have done our best." He said 17 company concessions had been revoked, 104 companies were under police investigation, 71,000 firefighters had been deployed and 16 people had died fighting the fires. The room has opened again.

scenario.shared_setting: Since August 2026, smoke haze from forest and land fires has drifted across Southeast Asia. Four ordinary people, each from a different country, take part in a public live audio room online where people from around the region talk about the haze. They do not know each other offline; the room opens again when there is news, and the same four keep turning up. Kelvin Tan is from Singapore, Farhana is from Malaysia, Budi Santoso is from Indonesia, and Nur Aqilah is from Brunei. Each lives in their own country and speaks from there, in English. None of them works for a government, a plantation or paper company, or an environmental group.

In Brunei, schools moved to home-based learning on 2 and 3 September.
